title: the leap decided
hook: the strongest one on the beach is the only one who hasn't said a word, and an old bear walks over to remind him who he is

segments.voice: Yesterday: yojana, part one. Ten, twenty, thirty, ninety, and your line, no one could promise a hundred and back. Did you give an honest number when someone asked? Today, the quiet one. Day six hundred three.

Some people never put their hand up. Not because they can't do the thing, but because it hasn't occurred to them that they could. Every team has one. On the beach, while the others were calling out their numbers, Hanuman sat to one side, silent. Valmiki doesn't give him a line in the whole count. So Jambavan, the oldest one there, the one who knows everybody's story, gets up, walks over, and sits down beside him.
screen: `HANUMAN SITS APART.` → `NOT ONE WORD IN THE COUNT.` → `JAMBAVAN WALKS OVER.`

segments.voice: What Jambavan does next is simple. He tells Hanuman his own story. Your mother, he says, was Anjana. Your father is Vayu, the wind. And when you were a baby, you saw the sun coming up and thought it was a ripe fruit, so you jumped for it, straight up into the sky. Indra, king of the gods, threw his thunderbolt, and you fell, and your jaw was struck. In Sanskrit the jaw is hanu, and that, Jambavan says, is where your name comes from. The wind god was so grieved that he stopped blowing, and the gods gave you gifts to set things right. Then Jambavan says the thing he came to say: you have your father's speed. Why are you sitting there? And Hanuman stands up. Valmiki describes him growing, filling with strength, roaring until the others cheer. He says he will leap the ocean, find Sita, and come back. Then he climbs Mount Mahendra by the shore to push off from. And that is where the Kishkindha Kanda, the book of the monkey kingdom, ends: on top of a mountain, before the jump. It's worth asking why Hanuman needed reminding at all. Valmiki's scene doesn't fully say. A curse in the Uttara Kanda, the last book, which many scholars think was added later, explains that sages once made him forget his strength until someone recalled it to him. Many families tell it that way. Either way, the scene holds: sometimes strength comes back when someone else remembers it out loud.
screen: `JAMBAVAN TELLS HIM HIS STORY.` · `THE SUN, THE THUNDERBOLT, THE JAW.` · `WHY ARE YOU SITTING THERE?` · then, large: `HANUMAN STANDS AND GROWS.` · then: `THE KISHKINDHA KANDA ENDS ON MAHENDRA.`

segments.voice: Settle and breathe. Think of someone you know who doesn't put their hand up: a friend, a sibling, a coworker who's better than they believe. Recall one specific thing they did well, a time you saw their strength. Hold that memory as you breathe. Then let the next breath come in a little fuller, as if you were holding the memory up for them to see. The bell holds the time.

Hanu, the Sanskrit word for jaw, struck by Indra's thunderbolt when Hanuman was a baby, and the source of his name, which Jambavan recalls to remind him of his father's speed before he rises and climbs Mount Mahendra.
Your line: why are you sitting there? Today, be someone's Jambavan: tell one person, plainly, a strength of theirs you've seen. Day six hundred three.

howItsDone: Jambavan reminding Hanuman of his strength is one of the best-known scenes in Hindu storytelling, and in many homes and temples it is told before the recitation of the Sundara Kanda begins.

fork.setup: you're Jambavan. the strongest monkey is sitting silent while the mission stalls. what do you do?
options: tell him his own story until he remembers his strength.
fork.reveal: Jambavan recounts Hanuman's birth and childhood, then asks why he's sitting there. Hanuman rises and grows.

original.note: Sanskrit hanumān, often explained as 'having a (notable) jaw', from hanu, jaw.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hanuman always knew he could fly across the sea.
what it means: in Valmiki, he sits silent until Jambavan reminds him of who he is.
what a scholar hears: the explanation that sages cursed him to forget his strength comes from the Uttara Kanda, a book many scholars date later than the core of the epic.

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
Birth story details (Anjana, Vayu, the sun as fruit, Indra's thunderbolt striking the jaw, Vayu's withdrawal, the gods' boons): confirm against Kishkindha 66.
The forgetting-curse: confirm its location (Uttara Kanda 36 in the vulgate) and the scholarly view of the Uttara Kanda as later.
Kanda boundary: Kishkindha closes here; Sundara opens tomorrow (day 604).
